author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Test PS2 emulation performance after an Android system update
summary: Re-run saved baseline routes after an Android update, recording build, driver, power policy, permissions, cache state, and cold versus warm behavior before attributing a regression to the emulator or changing many settings.
heroAlt: Official PCSX2 release banner representing a fresh software and system baseline after an update

sourceLabels.android-vulkan: Android Vulkan device and driver context

blocks.text: Recreate the pre-update baseline before tuning

A system update can change GPU drivers, schedulers, thermal policy, permissions, storage access, battery controls, or cache contents. The first launch may also rebuild graphics data and appear worse temporarily. Use the same game saves and route tables recorded before the update. Separate first launch, immediate replay, and sustained warm behavior before declaring a persistent regression.
Do not delete app data or rewrite all per-game profiles before preserving logs and the first post-update measurements. Those actions erase the most useful comparison evidence.
Collect old and new system identity

items: A pre-update route, profile, and timing record for at least one representative title.
Current Android build, security patch, GPU driver, and emulator version recorded.
Library, saves, and settings backed up before repair attempts.
Battery mode, display refresh, brightness, and vendor game mode matched.
A route containing both shader warm-up and sustained gameplay.

blocks.text: Separate rebuild cost from persistent regression

items: 1. Launch the title once and record permission, renderer, cache, and driver messages.
2. Run the baseline route as the first post-update pass and mark new hitches.
3. Replay immediately without changing settings to measure warm behavior.
4. Cool the device, cold-boot, and complete the sustained route again.
5. Verify folder access, battery policy, display refresh, and vendor game mode.
6. Compare one alternate stable renderer only when the baseline renderer remains abnormal.
7. Test a second representative title to distinguish global from title-specific behavior.
8. Create a dated regression record containing before and after system identity.

blocks.text: A first-pass-only problem commonly reflects cache rebuild or permission revalidation. A persistent change across warm and cold passes suggests driver, policy, or emulator interaction. A second title shows whether the effect follows the platform or one game profile.
The conclusion must survive warm-up and a repeated cold run with the prior baseline recreated faithfully.

items: Old and new Android and driver identity are recorded.
The exact pre-update game profile is restored.
First, repeat, and sustained passes are distinguished.
Permissions and power controls are verified explicitly.
At least two titles indicate the scope of the change.
App version also changes unnoticed: record it and begin a new baseline.
Caches are cleared between passes: repeat the lifecycle sequence.
The update resets display refresh or Battery Saver: match policy first.
Only one random scene is measured: use saved deterministic routes.

blocks.text: Restore the last verified renderer and per-game profiles, remove diagnostic overlays, and retain the backups and dated comparison. Do not attempt unsupported system downgrades as an ordinary emulator troubleshooting step; report the regression with reproducible evidence.
Driver identity may be hidden or vendor-specific

Some Android builds expose limited GPU-driver information or update components independently. Record every visible build and system component version and state clearly when the exact driver revision cannot be confirmed.
